item.title: Margaret Hamilton, computing pioneer who led software development for the Apollo program, dies at 90
item.description:
Over two decades at MIT, Hamilton forged new paths in computer science and engineering. Her groundbreaking work included leading the team that programmed the first computers that took humans to the moon.
A computing pioneer who authored over 130 publications, Hamilton helped to establish software engineering as a dedicated discipline. She worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, after which she became a successful computing entrepreneur and CEO. Her life’s work was recognized with many awards and honors, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, whose citation noted: “Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.” “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” says Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Margaret Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success. And for her that was just the beginning! She went on to become an entrepreneur and remained on the cutting edge of systems software throughout an extraordinary career, while acting as an advocate, mentor, and inspiration to millions.” https://news.mit.edu/2026/margaret-hamilton-computing-pioneer-dies-1007

item.title: Helped in a scary situation thanks for my cpr class
item.description: I heard the fire alarm going off across from me in my neighbors apartment. After a few moments, I went over to check on her. She asked me to call 911 and started to have a seizure due to sensory overload. The pizza she was trying to bake burnt a little. Luckily, due to the basic life support and cpr class, I knew exactly what to do and turned her on to her side, and timed the seizure and so on while on the phone with dispatch. Luckily, she is okay and recovering, receiving care. (There sounds like there is other medical stuff going on) This is just a reminder that it is always a good idea to attend or renew your local cpr or basic life support class.

item.title: NASA has released onboard video of Artemis II's reentry through Earth's atmosphere. Top speed: about 25,000 mph
item.description: https://www.reddit.com/r/interestingasfuck/s/Xz4O6O3rDL https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Koch Christina Koch mentioned that they made an agreement with eachother to stay as calm as possible if something goes wrong, even if that malfunction meant their deaths. During the reentry she couldnt properly hear commander Reid Wiseman when he called out their speeds and only heard snippets making her think they were going waaay too fast. Then she noticed everyone else was calm and thought everything must be fine. Then she remembered their agreement and realized thats exactly how they agreed to behave if something goes horribly wrong and got worried again. But she also noticed that the capsule did slow down a lot so she relaxed again. Quite the rollercoaster of emotions she went through during those 13min of reentry.
